evaluation.positioning_hook: A frustrated Flagstaff accountant makes a wish for a second life, then discovers the man who took it is living his family, his career, and his worst impulses.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean, sellable engine: midlife dissatisfaction, a supernatural bargain, and a home-invasion-style identity theft. The audience is real and the hook is easy to pitch, though the tonal swing into surreal horror narrows it from broad four-quadrant play.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The script announces its premise early with Champney’s nightmare, the green-eyed intruder, and the December 20th date. By the time Gene appears in Hollywood and the swap mechanics emerge, the central question is clear and sticky.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Champ is a strong lead because his shame, vanity, and longing are all legible in the office promotion scene and the fight with Cheyenne. Gene is also vivid, but the supporting family is more functional than deeply individualized outside of Gerry’s Lego obsession and Becky’s independence.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a familiar midlife-crisis setup and pushes it into body-swap-adjacent psychological horror with a movie-within-a-movie structure. The Flagstaff-to-Hollywood contrast, the green-eye mythology, and the final identity inversion give it a confident, off-kilter identity.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The first half builds well through the promotion disappointment, the bar encounter, and the first swap reveal. The middle section has strong escalation, though the repeated dream/reality reversals and production-set detours create some drag before the final confrontation.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea lands immediately: a man who wants out of his life gets exactly that, and the replacement is worse than he imagined. The emotional irony of Champ becoming the intruder in his own home gives the concept a memorable, inevitable sting.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Flagstaff is rendered with enough specificity to feel lived-in: the diner, the arthouse theater, the snowy commute, the accounting office, the Christmas residue. The Hollywood side adds a second texture layer, but the world is still primarily built to serve the central premise rather than generate many offshoots.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct blend of domestic melancholy, surreal menace, and satirical showbiz fantasy. The humming motif, the green-eyed imagery, and the abrupt shifts from intimate family drama to nightmare logic create a recognizable tonal signature.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are real thematic layers here around regret, masculinity, self-erasure, and the fantasy of reinvention. The Gene/Thomas backstory and the recurring date suggest more beneath the surface, though the script mostly delivers its meanings directly rather than withholding them.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Champ/Cheyenne/Gene is a strong triangle, and the family dynamic gives the script recurring friction. Still, the engine is heavily lead-driven, with the supporting players mostly orbiting Champ’s crisis rather than generating independent story energy.

lead_characters.name: Champ Granger
lead_characters.demographics: White male, late 40s to early 50s, married father, middle-class professional, Flagstaff resident.
lead_characters.hook: A burned-out accountant with a theater kid’s ego and a family man’s shame, Champ is trapped between the life he built and the life he thinks he deserved. He starts as a man who can barely say what he wants, then becomes someone willing to wish his family away, and finally someone forced to live with the cost of that wish. The role lives in contradiction: pathetic, vain, wounded, funny, and increasingly dangerous.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Shannon in Take Shelter or Joaquin Phoenix in Joker — a spiraling, interior man whose humiliation, volatility, and self-delusion become the entire performance. It gives an actor a full-body breakdown, then a late-stage transformation into something mythic and unsettling.

lead_characters.name: Gene Alterno
lead_characters.demographics: White male, 40s to 50s, physically imposing but adaptable, performer-to-suburban-father range.
lead_characters.hook: Gene is the seductive double: first a magnetic street performer, then a mild suburban husband who seems to have stepped into Champ’s life with eerie ease. He’s charming, wounded, and possibly monstrous, but the script keeps him just human enough to make the swap feel like a moral trap rather than a genre gimmick. He’s the kind of antagonist who can smile while tightening the knife.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Patrick Wilson in Insidious or Michael Keaton in Birdman a chance to play charisma with rot underneath. It offers a performer the rare pleasure of being both the wish fulfillment and the warning sign.

lead_characters.name: Cheyenne Granger
lead_characters.demographics: White female, 40s, wife, mother, artistically inclined, Flagstaff housewife with a latent creative life.
lead_characters.hook: Cheyenne is the emotional center Champ keeps failing to see clearly: practical, affectionate, frustrated, and more resilient than he gives her credit for. She reads as the woman who has built a life around compromise, but the painting thread and her final recognition of Champ give her a quiet inner life that matters. She’s not just the wife in the middle of the conflict; she’s the person the men keep trying to claim as proof of their worth.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Laura Dern in Marriage Story or Toni Collette in Hereditary a chance to play love, fatigue, and alarm in the same frame. It offers a strong actress the chance to be the emotional truth the movie keeps circling.

lead_characters.name: Gerry Granger
lead_characters.demographics: Male child, about 12, insecure, observant, emotionally guarded.
lead_characters.hook: Gerry is the son who sees more than the adults think, but not enough to understand what he’s seeing. His Lego castle, his discomfort with Champ, and his shifting loyalty to Gene give the movie a child’s-eye pressure point. He’s the most vulnerable piece in the family system, which makes every scene with him feel loaded.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of part that gave Jacob Tremblay in Room or Noah Jupe in A Quiet Place a chance to carry fear, confusion, and tenderness without overplaying it. It’s a real showcase for a young actor who can make silence feel active.

lead_characters.name: Becky Granger
lead_characters.demographics: Female teen, about 17, independent, sharp, socially aware.
lead_characters.hook: Becky is the oldest child and the quickest read in the room, the one who can puncture Champ’s self-mythology with a single line. She’s lightly sketched compared to the others, but she gives the family a teen-age skepticism that keeps the movie from becoming purely adult melodrama. Her green-eyed version of the family also makes her a key visual marker of the swap.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Kaitlyn Dever in Short Term 12 or Angourie Rice in The Nice Guys a chance to play intelligence and attitude without losing vulnerability. It’s a sharp supporting turn for a young actor who can land dry comedy and unease.

lead_characters.name: Trish
lead_characters.hook: Trish is the bridge between Champ’s fantasy life and the machinery that feeds it, always one step ahead of his confusion. She’s practical, loyal, and increasingly alarmed, which makes her the audience’s pressure valve inside the movie-business layer of the story. She also helps sell the surreal reveal by treating it like a normal workday until it isn’t.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Kathryn Hahn in Transparent or Jennifer Coolidge in Promising Young Woman a chance to make supporting material pop through timing and authority. It’s a smart, scene-stealing part for an actor who can keep the movie grounded while it gets stranger.

lead_characters.name: Mikey
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s to 40s, director, creative professional, self-assured but not fully in control.
lead_characters.hook: Mikey is the filmmaker inside the film, the person who turns Champ’s breakdown into product and then into prestige. He’s not written as a villain so much as a professional who believes the work justifies the chaos, which makes him a useful mirror for Champ’s own self-importance. His presence sharpens the movie’s satire of performance and authorship.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Paul Dano in The Fabelmans or Adam Driver in Marriage Story a chance to play intelligence, irritation, and authority in a contained space. It’s a strong supporting part for an actor who can make creative control feel seductive and slightly absurd.

lead_characters.name: Dan Huntington
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s, office rival, polished, socially successful.
lead_characters.hook: Dan is the office guy Champ resents because he embodies the version of adulthood that gets rewarded without visible suffering. He’s not especially complex on the page, but he’s useful as a human benchmark for Champ’s humiliation and later as a witness to the final transformation. He functions as the ordinary world Champ can’t tolerate being second in.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a character actor a clean, memorable lane like the office rivals in The Devil Wears Prada or The Office. It’s a compact part with a strong before-and-after contrast.

lead_characters.name: Todd
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 60s, boss, older professional authority figure.
lead_characters.hook: Todd is the blunt institutional gatekeeper who quietly crushes Champ’s promotion fantasy. He’s not flashy, but his calm dismissal is one of the script’s most effective humiliations because it’s so ordinary. He represents the world that keeps telling Champ to stay in his lane.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a veteran actor the pleasure of playing understatement with real consequence, like J.K. Simmons in Whiplash or Richard Jenkins in The Visitor. It’s a small but sharp authority role.

lead_characters.name: Sandy
lead_characters.demographics: Ambiguous gender presentation, teen to older adult, arthouse theater attendant.
lead_characters.hook: Sandy is a strange little hinge in the movie, half oracle and half theater clerk, giving Champ the ticket into the fantasy. The ambiguity is part of the texture, and the character’s deadpan delivery helps the film pivot from mundane to uncanny. Sandy feels like a minor character who knows more than they should.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of oddball role that can become a cult favorite, like the attendant in The Lighthouse or the clerk in Twin Peaks. It’s a small showcase for precise, offbeat line delivery.

casting_characteristics: Adult male lead requires strong emotional volatility and physical breakdown
Gene and Champ need enough resemblance in energy to sell the swap

notable_requirements: House interiors that can play as two different lives

technical.vfx_details: Primarily stylized transitions, eye-color/glow effects, dream-state imagery, and a few surreal visual beats; no large-scale VFX dependency.
technical.sfx_needs: Blood effects, knife wounds, broken glass, practical gore, snow/weather dressing, and a few controlled fight beats.

rights_flags.detail: Sunset Boulevard is specifically referenced as the arthouse theater marquee title.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best suited to a streamer-backed theatrical or specialty theatrical launch with strong genre marketing.

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly contained, but the script needs snow exteriors, a second-life Hollywood run, a movie-set layer, and repeated blood/gore resets that can add up.

casting.note: Champ has to carry humiliation, menace, comedy, and breakdown in one role, while Gene must read as both seductive and threatening; Gerry also needs a child actor who can hold emotional tension.

development.note: The premise is clear, but the repeated dream/swap/reveal structure and the movie-within-a-movie layer create a calibration challenge around how literal the supernatural rules are.

comp_set.title: The One I Love
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the identity-swap relationship tension and the way a domestic crisis becomes a genre puzzle.

comp_set.title: Beau Is Afraid
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the anxious male-lead spiral, surreal logic, and psychological dread around family and self-worth.

comp_set.title: The Invitation
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on the slow-burn unease, social discomfort, and the sense that a dinner-table reality is hiding something malignant.

comp_set.title: Birdman
comp_set.why_it_comps: The showbiz self-mythology, performance obsession, and actor-as-identity crisis are strongly adjacent.

comp_set.title: Black Swan
comp_set.why_it_comps: The psychological collapse, doubled identity, and bodily horror around ambition and self-erasure line up cleanly.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like elevated genre stories about midlife regret, identity collapse, and darkly comic psychological dread.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 25-54, slightly male-leaning but with strong female interest through the family/marriage angle; educated streaming audience and specialty theatrical viewers.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, modest cast, practical blood effects, and limited VFX keep it in indie feature territory despite the surreal scope.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where character breakdown and genre mechanics are both part of the sell. The script is built for buyers who want a strong lead role, a clear hook, and enough oddness to stand out in a crowded genre slate.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: the central swap is complete by the end, and no supporting character or world element is developed as a clean sequel or spinoff engine.

strengths.what_it_means: The movie has a clean commercial engine: a man gets the life he thinks he wants, then has to live inside the consequences. That makes it easy to pitch to buyers who want a genre hook with emotional stakes, and to actors who want a role built on contradiction.
strengths.evidence: Champ’s promotion humiliation, the bar confession, and the final realization that Gene has taken his place.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Champ is a real showcase role
strengths.what_it_means: The lead gives a performer humiliation, longing, comic self-delusion, and full psychological collapse in one package. That is exactly the kind of role that can attract a name actor or elevate a mid-career actor into a new lane.
strengths.evidence: The office scene, the fight with Cheyenne, the bar confession, and the final snowbound breakdown.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The family swap has emotional bite
strengths.what_it_means: The movie is not just about a curse; it’s about the terror of being replaced in your own home. That gives the genre mechanics a human ache that broadens the appeal beyond pure horror fans.
strengths.evidence: Gene living with Cheyenne and the kids, Champ being treated as a stranger, and the final porch confrontation.

strengths.what_it_means: The script has a built-in visual and tonal contrast between snowy domestic realism and neon showbiz fantasy. That helps the movie feel bigger than its footprint and gives marketing a strong before/after image.
strengths.evidence: The snowy house, the arthouse theater, Hollywood Boulevard, and the mansion fantasy sequences.

strengths.what_it_means: The humming motif, green-eye imagery, and surreal dream logic give the script a memorable signature. Buyers looking for elevated genre material can see a filmmaker’s voice rather than a generic thriller package.
strengths.evidence: The repeated tune, the green hue, the nightmare loops, and the final identity inversion.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, high-concept psychological thriller with a serious actor’s role at the center and a contained indie footprint underneath it. The script’s best commercial move is that it sells as both a genre hook and a midlife identity crisis, which makes it attractive to specialty buyers, streamer genre execs, and performers looking for a transformation piece.

items.area: The supernatural rules stay slippery for a long stretch.
items.detail: The script keeps the audience inside Champ’s confusion, which is effective, but it also means the mechanics of the swap, the dreams, and the green-eyed mythology are only partially legible until late. That creates a buyer conversation about whether the ambiguity is a feature or a friction point for mainstream genre audiences.

items.area: The middle section repeats the same emotional beat.
items.detail: Champ cycles through humiliation, confession, and partial revelation several times before the final confrontation, especially once the movie-set layer kicks in. The repetition helps the obsession theme, but it also risks flattening momentum in the back half of the feature.

items.area: Cheyenne and Becky are more functional than dimensional.
items.detail: Cheyenne carries the emotional stakes and Becky helps externalize the family replacement, but neither gets the same interior complexity as Champ or Gene. That matters because the ending depends on the family feeling like more than symbolic prizes in the men’s identity war.

items.area: The movie-set reveal changes the contract with the audience.
items.detail: The late pivot into a production set, director notes, and fake blood is a bold move, but it also re-frames the story after the audience has already invested in a more literal supernatural thriller. That’s a distinctive swing, but it will be a discussion point for buyers weighing clarity versus audacity.

items.area: Champ’s final turn is emotionally potent but morally extreme.
items.detail: By the end, he has crossed into attempted murder, public breakdown, and a new monstrous identity, which gives the climax force but also narrows sympathy. That’s a deliberate choice, but it makes the film more of a dark genre piece than a broadly empathetic prestige drama.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest friction is not the premise; it’s the calibration. The audience is asked to ride a deliberately unstable reality for most of the movie, and the late movie-set turn plus the repeated identity reversals will be the main buyer questions alongside the relatively thin family interiority.
